sections.title: Negative feedback
sections.text: Definition: negative feedback subtracts the measured output from the reference signal to form an error signal, and the controller acts to shrink that error. Example: a room thermostat measures 19 °C against a 21 °C set point, sees an error of 2 °C and switches the heater on until the error closes. Negative feedback usually reduces sensitivity to disturbances and to changes in the plant. Important exception: negative feedback does not guarantee stability. If the loop gain is too high or the measurement arrives with too much delay, a negative feedback loop can overshoot, oscillate or diverge. Always check stability separately.

sections.title: Stability
sections.text: Definition: a system is stable when every bounded input produces a bounded output, so the response settles instead of growing without limit. Example: after a step change in set point, a stable cruise control settles near the new speed, while an unstable one keeps swinging faster and slower with growing amplitude. Stability is a property of the whole loop: plant, controller, sensor and any delay together. Adding gain or delay can move a stable loop towards instability.

sections.title: Open-loop control
sections.text: Definition: an open-loop controller sends a command without measuring the result. Example: a toaster heats for a fixed time whether the bread is pale or burnt. Open-loop control is simple and cheap and cannot become unstable through feedback, but it cannot correct for disturbances or model errors that it never measures.

sections.title: Closed-loop control
sections.text: Definition: a closed-loop controller measures the output and uses the error between reference and measurement to adjust its command. Example: cruise control measures road speed and opens the throttle more when a hill slows the car. Compared with open-loop control, closed-loop control rejects disturbances and tolerates model errors, at the cost of a sensor and the need to check stability.

sections.title: Proportional control
sections.text: Definition: a proportional controller multiplies the current error by a gain Kp. Example: with Kp = 2, an error of 3 units produces a command of 6 units. Increasing Kp makes the response faster and usually reduces steady-state error, but it can increase overshoot. Proportional control alone generally leaves some steady-state error when the plant needs a constant non-zero command.

sections.title: Integral action
sections.text: Definition: integral action adds up the error over time and keeps changing the command until the accumulated error stops growing. Example: a level controller keeps opening the valve slowly while the tank stays below target. Integral action can remove steady-state error for constant set points and disturbances. When the actuator saturates, the integral keeps growing, which is called windup; anti-windup logic stops or limits the integrator while the actuator is at its limit.

sections.title: Derivative action
sections.text: Definition: derivative action responds to how fast the error is changing, which adds damping and can reduce overshoot. Example: as a robot arm approaches its target quickly, the derivative term eases the command before the arm arrives. Derivative action amplifies high-frequency measurement noise, so a noisy sensor can make the command jitter.

sections.title: Steady-state error
sections.text: Definition: steady-state error is the difference between the reference and the output after the transient response has died away. Example: a heater under proportional control settles at 20.5 °C when the set point is 21 °C, leaving a steady-state error of 0.5 °C. Integral action or a higher proportional gain can reduce it.
